title: TSMC’s CoWoS Capacity to Double by 2028—and Rivals Will Still Win Orders - Semiwiki
gist: TSMC is reportedly on track to double CoWoS advanced-packaging capacity from ~130,000 to ~260,000 300mm-equivalent wafers per month between end-2026 and 2028 as AI infrastructure demand shifts from a temporary shortage into a multiyear capacity cycle, but expanding package sizes, HBM/substrate/testing bottlenecks and larger multi-die designs mean the shortage persists and creates durable order opportunities for Intel Foundry's EMIB/Foveros packaging and OSAT players like Amkor and ASE rather than eliminating them as overflow suppliers.

themes.theme: CoWoS Capacity Expansion & the AI Demand Cycle

insights.claim: TSMC reportedly plans to double its Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS) capacity from approximately 130,000 300mm-equivalent wafers per month at the end of 2026 to 260,000 by 2028.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A doubling of advanced-packaging capacity in two years is one of the largest capex-driven capacity buildouts in the AI supply chain and should be tracked as a leading indicator of TSMC's advanced-packaging capex trajectory and AI accelerator supply growth.

insights.claim: This capacity figure is not formal TSMC guidance but a supply-chain projection, so it should be treated as an estimate rather than confirmed company disclosure.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Investors should treat the 260,000 wafer/month 2028 figure as directional supply-chain-sourced intelligence, not an auditable guidance number, when building capacity models.
insights.quote: The estimate is not formal company guidance and should be treated as a supply-chain projection.
insights.locator: The estimate is not formal company guidance

insights.claim: The direction of TSMC's CoWoS expansion indicates that AI infrastructure demand is evolving from a temporary shortage into a multiyear capacity cycle rather than a short-lived supply crunch.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Reframes AI hardware supply constraints as a structural, multi-year capex cycle rather than a transient bottleneck, supporting sustained investment theses in packaging, substrate and testing capacity across the supply chain.

insights.claim: CoWoS is a family of 2.5D packaging technologies that places logic dies such as GPUs or custom accelerators together with high-bandwidth memory on a silicon interposer or redistribution-layer structure, enabling much higher bandwidth, lower latency and better energy efficiency than routing signals across a conventional circuit board.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Explains the technical mechanism by which packaging, not just transistor scaling, now gates AI accelerator performance — a key lens for evaluating any AI chip vendor's real deliverable performance.

insights.claim: Advanced packaging is essential to AI performance because leading accelerators require several HBM stacks to keep thousands of compute units supplied with data, meaning a faster processor has limited value if memory bandwidth, interconnect density or power delivery cannot scale with it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Packaging capacity, not raw wafer starts, is becoming the binding constraint on how many usable AI accelerators can reach the market — a key variable for modeling Nvidia/AMD/custom-ASIC shipment ceilings.

insights.claim: CoWoS is no longer simply the final step after wafer fabrication; it increasingly determines how much useful compute can be extracted from leading-edge silicon.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Investors valuing AI chip designers should weight packaging capacity access as heavily as wafer-node access when assessing supply security and margin durability.
insights.quote: CoWoS therefore is not simply the final step after wafer fabrication; it increasingly determines how much useful compute can be extracted from leading-edge silicon.

themes.theme: Expanding Package Sizes Offset Capacity Gains

insights.claim: TSMC certified a CoWoS solution supporting interposers measuring 5.5 times the maximum mask or reticle area in 2025, with volume production planned for 2026, allowing larger packages to accommodate more compute chiplets, I/O dies and HBM stacks.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Reticle-busting interposer sizes are a concrete technical milestone enabling next-gen multi-chiplet AI accelerators (e.g., rack-scale superchips); track TSMC's 2026 volume-production ramp of this format as a gating event for next-gen accelerator launches.
insights.quote: TSMC says it certified a CoWoS solution supporting interposers measuring 5.5 times the maximum mask or reticle area in 2025, with volume production planned for 2026.

insights.claim: Because larger CoWoS packages consume more interposer area and packaging resources per device, doubling wafer-equivalent CoWoS capacity does not necessarily double the number of completed accelerators produced.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A critical nuance for unit-shipment forecasting: naive extrapolation from wafer-capacity doubling to accelerator-unit doubling will overstate actual chip supply growth.
insights.quote: Consequently, doubling wafer-equivalent capacity does not necessarily double the number of completed accelerators.

insights.claim: TSMC's 2025 annual report identifies CoWoS, InFO and SoIC as central technologies for large-scale, power-efficient integration, signaling these packaging platforms are core to TSMC's strategic roadmap, not peripheral offerings.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Confirms TSMC's own capital allocation priority is shifting materially toward advanced packaging alongside wafer fabrication.

insights.claim: The CoWoS expansion should help Nvidia, AMD and custom-ASIC developers raise shipments, yet it may not eliminate the AI accelerator shortage because AI clusters are moving toward larger multi-die packages while hyperscalers simultaneously develop internal accelerators alongside purchasing merchant GPUs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Demand is growing in both volume and packaging intensity simultaneously, meaning capacity additions get absorbed faster than headline numbers suggest — supports a bullish multi-year view on packaging capex names even as nominal capacity rises.

insights.claim: Yield management, HBM availability, substrates, thermal solutions and testing capacity can remain bottlenecks in AI chip supply even when nominal CoWoS wafer output rises.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Investors should monitor the full packaging value chain — substrates, thermal solutions, test capacity, HBM supply — not just CoWoS wafer counts, as each is an independent potential choke point on AI chip supply.
insights.quote: Yield management, HBM availability, substrates, thermal solutions and testing capacity can remain bottlenecks even when nominal CoWoS output rises.

themes.theme: Openings for Intel Foundry and OSAT Second Sources

insights.claim: Persistent CoWoS supply constraints create an opening for Intel Foundry, whose Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB) places small silicon bridges inside the package substrate instead of using a large interposer beneath every die, while Foveros adds vertical die stacking and EMIB-T combines bridge-based connections with through-silicon vias.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Intel Foundry has a genuine alternative packaging technology stack that could win custom-accelerator business precisely because TSMC's CoWoS remains capacity-constrained — a competitive-positioning catalyst worth tracking for Intel Foundry customer wins.

insights.claim: Intel's EMIB, EMIB-T and Foveros packaging technologies are not drop-in replacements for every CoWoS design; customers must separately qualify physical interfaces, assembly processes, thermal behavior and reliability before switching.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Switching costs and qualification cycles will slow, not block, share shifts toward Intel Foundry packaging — temper near-term expectations of rapid share capture despite the capacity opening.
insights.locator: These technologies are not drop-in replacements

insights.claim: Intel has confirmed its advanced-packaging portfolio includes EMIB, EMIB-T and Foveros, while MediaTek has publicly stated it supports both Intel and TSMC packaging platforms.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: MediaTek's public dual-sourcing stance is a concrete early proof point that fabless customers are actively hedging packaging supplier concentration risk away from TSMC alone.
insights.locator: Intel has confirmed that its advanced-packaging

insights.claim: Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) providers such as ASE and Amkor should capture spillover packaging demand by performing package assembly, bumping, substrate integration and final testing, either in cooperation with foundries or through competing 2.5D platforms.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: OSAT names are a direct way to gain exposure to AI packaging capacity tightness without foundry-level capital intensity or node risk.

insights.claim: Amkor's Arizona advanced-packaging campus is scheduled to begin production in 2028, illustrating how AI-driven packaging demand is also encouraging geographic diversification of the supply chain away from Asia concentration.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated data point (2028 start) for tracking US-based advanced-packaging capacity coming online — relevant to CHIPS Act-style reshoring theses and geopolitical supply-chain risk reduction.
insights.quote: Amkor’s Arizona advanced-packaging campus, scheduled to begin production in 2028, illustrates how packaging demand is also encouraging geographic diversification.

insights.claim: Semiconductor industry leadership is no longer defined solely by transistor density; the ability to combine heterogeneous dies, HBM and high-speed interfaces at acceptable yield and cost now determines accelerator supply.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A framework shift for evaluating foundry competitiveness: packaging/integration capability is becoming as strategically important as leading-edge node access, which should reweight how investors compare TSMC, Intel Foundry and Samsung Foundry.
insights.quote: Semiconductor leadership is no longer defined solely by transistor density.

insights.claim: TSMC's CoWoS expansion reinforces its leadership, but persistent demand gives Intel Foundry and OSAT providers something equally valuable: production orders, customer qualifications, and the opportunity to become permanent second sources rather than temporary overflow suppliers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The key investable conclusion: TSMC stays the leader, but the shortage itself is durably valuable to alternative suppliers, favoring a diversified long thesis across TSMC, Intel Foundry and OSAT rather than TSMC alone.
insights.quote: TSMC’s expansion reinforces its leadership, but persistent demand gives Intel and OSAT providers something equally valuable—production orders, customer qualifications and the opportunity to become permanent second sources rather than temporary overflow suppliers.
